**Morales Defends Expulsion of U.S. Ambassador, Says Bolivia Seeks Better Ties Under Obama**

**La Paz, Bolivia — April 2009**

Bolivian President Evo Morales defended his government’s decision to expel the United States ambassador last year, saying in an interview with **CNN en Español** that the move was necessary to protect Bolivia’s sovereignty, while also expressing hope that relations with Washington could improve under President Barack Obama.

Morales, Bolivia’s first Indigenous president and a close ally of Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez, said the September 2008 expulsion of U.S. Ambassador **Philip Goldberg** was not an act of hostility toward the American people but a response to what his government viewed as interference in Bolivia’s internal affairs.

“We want relations based on mutual respect,” Morales said during the interview, arguing that no foreign government should support political movements aimed at destabilizing an elected administration.

The Morales government accused Goldberg of maintaining improper contacts with opposition leaders during a period of intense unrest in Bolivia’s eastern lowland departments, where conservative regional governors were resisting the president’s socialist reforms and demands for greater state control over natural resources. Washington denied the allegations, calling the ambassador’s expulsion unjustified.

The diplomatic rupture marked one of the lowest points in U.S.-Bolivian relations in decades. Following Goldberg’s departure, the United States expelled Bolivia’s ambassador in Washington, and Morales later ordered the suspension of operations by the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration in Bolivia, accusing DEA agents of political meddling. U.S. officials also denied those accusations.

In his CNN en Español appearance, Morales sought to draw a distinction between his criticisms of past U.S. policy and his view of the new Obama administration. He said the change of government in Washington created an opportunity to rebuild ties, provided the United States recognized Bolivia’s right to make independent decisions.

“With President Obama, there is hope,” Morales said in substance, while emphasizing that any renewed relationship must be “from government to government” and “with respect for dignity and sovereignty.”

Morales said Bolivia remained willing to cooperate with the United States on trade, development and anti-drug efforts, but rejected what he described as policies of pressure or conditional assistance. He defended Bolivia’s approach to coca cultivation, saying the coca leaf is a traditional Andean crop and should not be equated automatically with cocaine trafficking.

The Bolivian president has long promoted the slogan “coca yes, cocaine no,” arguing that his government can combat drug trafficking while protecting Indigenous and peasant farmers who cultivate coca for legal and traditional uses. U.S. officials have repeatedly expressed concern that reduced DEA involvement could weaken anti-narcotics operations, though Bolivian authorities insist they are capable of carrying out their own enforcement strategy.

The interview came as Morales was consolidating political power ahead of general elections scheduled for December 2009. Earlier in the year, Bolivian voters approved a new constitution that expanded Indigenous rights, increased state authority over natural resources and allowed Morales to seek another term.

Opposition leaders in Bolivia accused Morales of using anti-American rhetoric to rally his political base and distract from domestic tensions. Supporters, however, said his stance reflected a broader regional rejection of U.S. influence in Latin America and a demand for more equal relations.

Morales’ comments also coincided with a period of cautious diplomatic outreach between the Obama administration and several left-leaning Latin American governments. Obama, who took office in January 2009, had signaled a desire for a new tone in the region, though disputes over drug policy, trade, democracy and relations with Venezuela and Cuba continued to complicate Washington’s ties with governments such as Bolivia’s.

Despite the sharp break of 2008, Morales’ remarks suggested that La Paz was not closing the door on reconciliation. The central condition, he said, was that the United States abandon any attempt to influence Bolivia’s domestic politics.

“We are not against the United States,” Morales said, according to the thrust of his comments. “We are against intervention.”

**Morales Uses U.N. Earth Day Platform to Denounce Capitalism, Warn of Foreign-Backed Efforts to Divide Bolivia**

**UNITED NATIONS / LA PAZ** — Bolivian President Evo Morales used an Earth Day appearance at the United Nations to cast the global environmental crisis as a consequence of capitalism and consumerism, while also warning that his government faced what he described as a foreign-backed campaign by armed groups and opposition forces seeking to fracture Bolivia along regional and political lines.

Speaking at U.N. headquarters during events marking Earth Day, Morales called for a sweeping rethinking of the world economic order, arguing that the planet’s survival depends on replacing what he called a system driven by profit with one rooted in solidarity, respect for nature and the rights of Indigenous peoples.

“The Earth does not belong to us; we belong to the Earth,” Morales told delegates, presenting his remarks as both an environmental appeal and a political indictment of wealthy industrialized countries. He said climate change, food shortages and water scarcity were not isolated crises but symptoms of an economic model that treats natural resources as commodities rather than common goods.

Morales, Bolivia’s first Indigenous president and a former coca growers’ union leader, urged governments to recognize the “rights of Mother Earth” and accused developed nations of consuming far beyond sustainable limits while asking poorer countries to bear the burden of environmental protection. He called for reductions in excessive consumption, stronger protections for biodiversity and water, and an end to policies that, in his view, prioritize corporate interests over human life and ecological balance.

But Morales’ address went beyond climate diplomacy. In remarks that underscored the deepening political confrontation at home, he alleged that Bolivia’s democratic transformation was being challenged by foreign-backed gunmen and domestic opposition leaders determined to weaken or divide the country.

According to Morales, armed groups had been encouraged or supported by interests outside Bolivia and were working in coordination with conservative opposition forces in the country’s eastern lowlands, where regional leaders had pushed for greater autonomy from the central government. He framed those efforts as part of a broader attempt to derail his administration’s program of nationalizing natural resources, redistributing land and elevating Indigenous political power.

“They do not forgive us for recovering our natural resources,” Morales said in substance, referring to his government’s moves to increase state control over gas and other strategic sectors. He accused opponents of using demands for autonomy as a cover for separatism, particularly in wealthier eastern departments such as Santa Cruz, Tarija, Beni and Pando, where resistance to his government has been strongest.

Opposition leaders in Bolivia have repeatedly denied that they are seeking to break up the country, saying their autonomy movement is intended to decentralize power, protect regional revenues and resist what they describe as Morales’ concentration of authority in La Paz. They have also accused the president of using allegations of conspiracy to discredit legitimate political dissent.

Morales’ accusations reflect a period of intense polarization in Bolivia, where his government’s efforts to rewrite the constitution, expand Indigenous rights and assert greater state control over the economy have been met by protests, regional referendums and confrontations between government supporters and opposition activists. The autonomy movement in the eastern lowlands has drawn support from business groups, ranchers and local political elites who fear losing influence under Morales’ reforms.

At the United Nations, Morales linked those domestic disputes to global struggles over resources, sovereignty and economic power. He said Bolivia’s campaign to defend the environment and reclaim control over gas, minerals and land had provoked resistance from powerful interests both inside and outside the country. In his telling, the defense of “Mother Earth” and the defense of Bolivian unity were part of the same struggle.

The Bolivian leader has frequently accused the United States and other foreign actors of interfering in his country’s internal affairs, though such claims have often been disputed by Washington and by Morales’ domestic critics. U.S. officials have denied supporting separatism or armed destabilization efforts in Bolivia, saying they support democracy and constitutional processes.

Morales’ Earth Day message resonated with many developing-country diplomats and environmental activists who have long argued that climate negotiations must account for historical responsibility and global inequality. His language also reflected an emerging Bolivian diplomatic campaign to place Indigenous concepts of ecological balance at the center of international climate debates.

“Mother Earth is not merchandise,” Morales said, warning that market-based approaches alone would not solve climate change. He urged the international community to move beyond what he described as symbolic environmental commitments and adopt binding policies to protect forests, reduce emissions and guarantee access to water as a human right.

His remarks came as climate change was increasingly rising on the global agenda, with governments debating how to craft a successor framework to the Kyoto Protocol and how to balance emissions reductions with development needs. Morales argued that poor countries should not be forced to choose between poverty and environmental preservation, saying industrialized nations must assume greater responsibility for financing climate adaptation and changing consumption patterns.

For Morales, the international and domestic fronts appeared inseparable. He presented Bolivia as a country attempting to chart an alternative path: one based on Indigenous values, state control of strategic resources and resistance to foreign pressure. At the same time, he portrayed his government as under siege from adversaries who, he said, opposed those transformations and were prepared to use violence or regional division to stop them.

The result was a speech that combined environmental advocacy, anti-capitalist critique and a warning about Bolivia’s internal stability. On Earth Day, Morales sought to position himself not only as a defender of the planet, but also as the leader of a country whose political future, he argued, was being contested by forces tied to the same global system he blamed for ecological destruction.

Whether his allegations will gain traction beyond his political base remains uncertain. Supporters see Morales as defending national sovereignty against entrenched elites and foreign interference. Critics say he is deepening divisions by branding opponents as conspirators. But at the United Nations, Morales made clear that he views Bolivia’s environmental agenda, economic nationalism and territorial unity as parts of a single battle — one he insists has implications far beyond his country’s borders.

**UNITED NATIONS —** Bolivian President Evo Morales defended his government’s confrontational stance toward Washington on Wednesday, saying his decision to expel the U.S. ambassador was necessary to protect Bolivia’s sovereignty amid escalating political unrest.

Morales, Bolivia’s first Indigenous president, accused U.S. Ambassador Philip Goldberg of supporting opposition groups seeking to destabilize his government. Washington denied the allegations and responded by expelling Bolivia’s ambassador, deepening tensions between the two countries.

The diplomatic dispute unfolded as Morales faced fierce opposition from governors and civic leaders in Bolivia’s eastern lowlands, particularly in the wealthy Santa Cruz region, where critics accused him of concentrating power and threatening regional autonomy.

Violence linked to the political crisis culminated in a deadly firefight in Santa Cruz, where Bolivian authorities said they had disrupted a plot against the president. Opposition figures questioned the government’s account, while officials insisted the operation exposed a serious threat to national security.

Speaking at the United Nations, Morales broadened his message beyond Bolivia’s domestic turmoil, urging world leaders to recognize and defend the rights of “Mother Earth.” He called for a new global approach to environmental protection, arguing that capitalism and unchecked industrial development had harmed the planet and Indigenous communities.

“The Earth does not belong to us,” Morales said in remarks emphasizing Indigenous traditions and environmental stewardship. “We belong to the Earth.”

Morales’ speech underscored his effort to frame Bolivia’s struggles as part of a wider battle over sovereignty, natural resources and the global economic order — themes that have defined his presidency and strained relations with the United States.
